courses.title: Jobava London
courses.sub: 1.d4, 2.Nc3 and 3.Bf4: one simple attacking set-up for White against almost everything
courses.why: The Jobava London gives you the same first three moves in nearly every game, so you spend your time on plans, not on memorising. The knight on c3 and the bishop on f4 work together against c7, and many Black players at your level have never seen it. Against best play the position is about equal, but you know the plans and they usually don't. You already reach these positions often: in your games 1.d4 d5 is by far Black's most common answer.

ideas.text: Against ...d5 you play d4, Nc3 and Bf4 first, then e3. The bishop comes out before e3 so it is not locked in behind your pawns.

The knight jumps to b5 when c7 can only be guarded by the clumsy ...Na6, or when it wins something. After ...Nc6 Black cannot defend c7 with ...c6, so Nb5 is very strong. If Black can answer ...c6 comfortably, do not jump.
When Black plays ...e6 before ...Bf5 or ...c5, play Nb5 right away, before Black gets ...Bd6 or ...Bb4 in comfortably.
Offer to trade your light-squared bishop for Black's best piece. After the trade: Nf3, castle short and push e4.
Guard d4 with e3. If Black takes on d4, take back with the e-pawn. Take on c5 when Black's dark-squared bishop would have to move twice to win the pawn back.
The queen on d3 breaks the pin on your knight, guards e4 and b5, and prepares a3 and castling long.

ideas.t: No pawn on d5? Take the centre
ideas.text: If Black does not put a pawn on d5 (King's Indian, Pirc, Modern, ...b6), grab the whole centre with e4. Then Bf4, Qd2, castle long and attack with Bh6 and the h-pawn.
1. A knight on e5 supported by the f-pawn. 2. The e3-e4 pawn break once your pieces are out. 3. The bishop pair after Nxd6. 4. Castle long and push pawns against a fianchetto king.

structures.t: Black took on d4: pawns c3 and d4
structures.text: After ...cxd4 exd4 your d4 pawn is backed up by c3 and cannot be attacked by a Black pawn. The e5 square is yours: put a knight there, guarded by the bishop on f4. Black has the half-open c-file (no pawn of Black's on it) and will try to attack along it. Your plan is to castle, keep the knight on e5 and use the e-file.

structures.t: Black took the bishop on f4: pawns d4 and f4
structures.text: When Black swaps bishops on f4 and you take back with the e-pawn, the pawns on d4 and f4 make e5 a perfect home for your knight: no Black pawn can chase it. Black no longer has a dark-squared bishop, so the dark squares around Black's king are thin. Plan: castle, Ne5, then Qf3 or Qe2 and a rook to the e-file.

structures.t: Pawns on d4 and e4 against a fianchetto
structures.text: Against the King's Indian set-up you own the centre with two pawns. The kings are on opposite sides, so both sides attack. Yours is faster: Bh6 swaps off Black's best defender, then the h-pawn runs to h5 to open the h-file.

structures.t: Black's Dutch Stonewall: pawns d5, e6 and f5
structures.text: Black's pawns on d5, e6 and f5 leave a big hole on e5. Your bishop on f4 already controls it and a knight will land there. Black's light-squared bishop is stuck behind its own pawns.

structures.t: The light bishops are gone: d4 against d5
structures.text: After Bd3 and the swap of light-squared bishops the centre is level. Your queen on d3 eyes the light squares, your bishop on f4 is still active, and your plan is Nf3, castle short and push e3-e4 to open the game.

chapters.title: Black hits the centre: 3...c5
chapters.intro: Black attacks your d4 pawn at once. The rule: play e3 first, and if Black takes on d4, take back with the e-pawn. Then develop quickly and use the e5 square.

chapters.title: The solid 3...e6
chapters.intro: The most common reply at your level. Black plans ...Bd6 or ...Bb4 next. The rule: jump to b5 at once, before Black's bishop gets out comfortably.

chapters.title: Black develops the bishop: ...Bf5
chapters.intro: Black brings the light-squared bishop to f5 before playing ...e6. Your answer is always e3 and Bd3: offer to trade it, because it is Black's best minor piece. Take back on d3 with the c-pawn when Black's pawn is still on c7, and with the queen after ...c6.

chapters.title: Waiting moves, fianchetto and 3...Nc6
chapters.intro: Black plays a waiting move (...a6), a fianchetto (...g6) or the knight to c6. Against ...a6 your knight cannot use b5, so develop normally. Against ...g6 and ...Nc6 the Nb5 trick is back.

chapters.title: Black plays ...e6, ...c5, ...c6 or ...Nc6 before ...Nf6
chapters.intro: Black does not play ...Nf6 at once. You still play Nc3 and Bf4 (the system), then e3. Against ...e6 Black's dark-squared bishop often swaps itself off on f4: take back with the e-pawn and use the e5 square.

chapters.title: No pawn on d5: King's Indian, Modern, Philidor, Benoni and 1...Nf6 2.Nc3 e6
chapters.intro: If Black does not put a pawn on d5, take the whole centre with e4. Against the King's Indian and the Modern play Bf4, Qd2, castle long and attack with Bh6 and the h-pawn. Against ...e5 set-ups (Philidor) develop with Nf3, Bc4 and castle short. Against ...c5 push past with d5.

chapters.title: Dutch, Englund and other first moves
chapters.intro: Some players avoid 1...d5 and 1...Nf6. Against the Dutch (1...f5) the bishop goes to g5, not f4, but against the Stonewall (...d5) it goes to f4 as usual. Against 1...b6 take the centre with e4. After 1...e6 2.Nc3 hit back with d5 or Qd3. Against the Englund Gambit (1...e5) you take the pawn and keep it with simple developing moves.

lines.title: Main line: 4...cxd4 5.exd4 a6
lines.intro: Black's most accurate set-up: take on d4 and stop your knight with ...a6. The game is equal, but your plan is easy: Ne5, then a rock-solid pawn chain c3-d4 and a strong knight on d4.

lines.title: 6...Bg4: the bishop for the knight
lines.intro: Black pins your knight instead of playing ...Nc6. Kick the bishop with h3; after Black takes on f3 you have the two bishops and a queen ready for a kingside attack.

lines.title: 4...e6: the Nb5 jump
lines.intro: Black plays ...e6 and ...c5. Your knight jumps to b5 at once and hits c7, so Black must put a knight on the poor a6 square. (The same position comes from 3...e6 4.Nb5 Na6 5.e3 c5.)

lines.title: 4...a6: take on c5
lines.intro: Black plays ...a6 before taking on d4. Now you take on c5 yourself and hold the extra pawn with Na4 and b4. Remember the trick 8.c6!: the pawn attacks the knight on d7.

lines.title: 4...a6 5.dxc5 Qa5: castle long and attack
lines.intro: After 5.dxc5 the most accurate reply is ...Qa5: the queen pins your knight and wins the pawn back. Develop, castle long and start a pawn storm on the kingside. About equal and very lively.

lines.title: The Nb5 trick: 4...Nc6?
lines.intro: Black develops the knight to c6 too early. Now ...c6 is impossible, so nothing can cover c7 comfortably. Remember: Nb5 at once, with the fork on c7 in the air.

lines.title: Main line: 4.Nb5 Na6 5.e3 c6
lines.intro: Black guards c7 with the knight on a6 and then kicks your knight with ...c6. Remember: Nb5 first, e3 next, the knight goes back to c3, then a3, Nf3, Ne5. The game is about equal, but Black's knight on a6 is badly placed.

lines.title: 4...Bd6: take the bishop
lines.intro: Half of all players at your level answer Nb5 with ...Bd6. Take the bishop at once: you get the bishop pair for free. Remember: c3, Nf3, Be2 and castle; keep the bishop on the g5-h4-g3 diagonal.

lines.title: 4.Nb5 Na6 5.e3 Be7
lines.intro: Black develops the bishop to e7 and castles before kicking your knight. Develop with Nf3 and h3, go back to c3 when Black plays ...c6, then guard b2 with a3 and Rb1, as in the main line. About equal.

lines.title: 4.Nb5 Na6 5.e3 Bd7
lines.intro: Black guards b5 with the bishop instead of kicking your knight with ...c6. Support the knight with a4, then c3 and Bd3, and push the h-pawn when Black castles. About equal, but your pieces are more active.

lines.title: The fork: 4...c6??
lines.intro: Black kicks your knight with ...c6, but the c-pawn has left c7. Remember: when c7 is empty, Nc7+ forks the king and the rook.

lines.title: 3...Bf5 4.e3 e6 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.cxd3
lines.intro: The most common way: Black swaps bishops on d3. Take back with the c-pawn: it opens the c-file for your rook and your queen comes to b3 to hit b7. About equal, with clear plans.

lines.title: 5...Bxd3 6.cxd3 c5
lines.intro: Black hits d4 at once. Use the queen on b3 and the Nb5 jump: Black's knight has to go to a6 again.

lines.title: 5...Bg6: Black keeps the bishop
lines.intro: Black does not want to trade and steps back to g6. You take on g6 yourself, castle, and when Black swaps on f4 you get the f4-pawn clamp. The game is about equal.

lines.title: 3...c6 4.e3 Bf5 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.Qxd3
lines.intro: A Caro-Kann style set-up: ...c6 and ...Bf5. Trade bishops, take back with the queen this time, castle short and break with e4.

lines.title: 3...c6 4.e3 Bg4 5.f3 Bh5?!
lines.intro: Black pins nothing yet but puts the bishop on g4. Kick it with f3. Most players then retreat to h5, and your kingside pawns chase the bishop with h4 and g4. You win space and keep the safer king.

lines.title: 3...a6 4.e3 Bf5 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.cxd3
lines.intro: Black plays ...a6 first and then ...Bf5. Trade bishops and take back with the c-pawn: the queen goes to b3 and the rook to c1. You played 5.Bd3 in your games here and won; avoid 5.Nf3, which lets Black keep the strong bishop.

lines.title: 3...c6 4.e3 Qb6
lines.intro: Black's queen hits b2 at once. Guard it with the rook and develop. The game is about equal.

lines.title: Move-order: 2...Bf5
lines.intro: Black brings the bishop out on move two. Play 3.Bf4 and 4.e3 as always. The most common reply is ...Bb4: develop with Bd3 and Ne2, then swap bishops on d6.

lines.title: 3...a6 4.e3 e6
lines.intro: Black stops Nb5 with ...a6 and then plays ...e6 and ...c5. Take on c5 so that Black's bishop has to move twice, then castle and meet the queenside pawns with a4. Honest verdict: about equal.

lines.title: 3...a6 4.e3 Nc6
lines.intro: Black plays ...a6 and ...Nc6. Nb5 is not possible, so develop with Nf3 and keep your bishop safe from ...Nh5.

lines.title: 3...g6: Black fianchettoes
lines.intro: Black puts the bishop on g7. Use the Nb5 trick once more: Black has to put a knight on a6 before castling. Then go back to c3, play h3, Be2 and castle. About equal, with an easy plan.

lines.title: 3...g6 4.e3 Bg7 5.Nb5 O-O?
lines.intro: Black castles without thinking about c7. Take the pawn with the knight: it forks the queen and the rook.

lines.title: 3...Nc6?: Nb5 and the e5 gambit
lines.intro: One in five players at your level answers 3.Bf4 with ...Nc6. It blocks the c-pawn, so c7 cannot be guarded by ...c6. Jump to b5 at once. Black's best try is the gambit ...e5: take with the bishop, then with the pawn, and you win a pawn.

lines.title: 2...e6 3.Bf4 Bd6: the f4 clamp
lines.intro: Black offers to swap dark-squared bishops. Let Black take on f4 and recapture with the e-pawn: the pawns on d4 and f4 make e5 a home for your knight. Then Qd2, castle long and attack with the h-pawn.

lines.title: 2...e6 3.Bf4 Bb4: the queen to d3
lines.intro: Black pins your knight with ...Bb4. The answer is Qd3: the queen guards the knight, and a3 and later castling long take the sting out of the pin. Then b4 and the e4 break.

lines.title: 2...e6 3.Bf4 a6?!
lines.intro: Black stops your knight jump with ...a6. Play e3 and Nf3; after ...c5 and ...Nf6 take on c5, and the game is the same as in the line 3...a6 4.e3 e6.

lines.title: 2...e6 3.Bf4 Nc6: the bishop pair
lines.intro: Black puts the knight on c6, so c7 has no pawn guard. After e3 and ...Nf6 jump to b5 and take the d6 bishop: you get the two bishops. You lost both of your games from this position; with c3 and Be2 the game soon becomes the same as the line 3...e6 4.Nb5 Bd6.

lines.title: 2...c5: take on d4 with the queen
lines.intro: Black hits d4 at once on move two. After 3.Bf4 cxd4 take back with the queen. Watch the trick 5.Bxb8! and 7.Qxa7: you grab a pawn on the queenside.

lines.title: 2...c5 3.Bf4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6?
lines.intro: Black chases your queen with ...Nc6, but forgets that d5 is no longer guarded. Take the pawn.

lines.title: 2...Nc6
lines.intro: Black brings the knight to c6 on move two. Play 3.Bf4 and use the Nb5 trick: the knight on c6 blocks Black's c-pawn.

lines.title: 1...c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Bf4 Bf5
lines.intro: Black plays ...c6 and ...d5 (a Caro-Kann style set-up, also reached by 1...d5 2.Nc3 c6) and brings the bishop to f5 before ...Nf6. Play e3 and Bd3 as always; if Black keeps the bishop on f5, take it yourself. About equal.

lines.title: 2...c6 3.Bf4 Qb6
lines.intro: After 1...d5 2.Nc3 c6 3.Bf4 the queen comes to b6 at once and hits b2. Guard it with Rb1, develop, and take on f5 when Black brings the bishop there. About equal.

lines.title: 1...Nf6 2.Nc3 e6?! 3.Bf4 Bb4
lines.intro: After 1...Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 stay in the system with 3.Bf4. If Black pins with ...Bb4, Qd3 again. The position soon becomes the same as in the line 2...e6 3.Bf4 Bb4.

lines.title: 1...Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Bf4 c5: push to d5
lines.intro: Black hits d4 with ...c5. Push the pawn to d5. If Black swaps twice on d5, take back with the queen, castle long and swap queens: a calm, equal endgame where your pieces are easier to play.

lines.title: 1...Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.Bf4 b6?!: take the centre
lines.intro: Black wants a bishop on b7 but has not played ...d5. Take the centre with e4 at once. If Black pins with ...Bb4, push e5 and hit g7 with the queen: a forced sequence that leaves you with the two bishops.

lines.title: King's Indian: the big-centre attack
lines.intro: Black plays ...g6, ...d6, ...Bg7 and castles short. You build the big centre with e4, then Bf4, Qd2, castle long and attack with Bh6 and the h-pawn. White is clearly better.

lines.title: The Modern: 1...g6 2.e4 Bg7
lines.intro: Black fianchettoes before playing ...Nf6. Take the centre with e4, then Nc3, Bf4, Qd2 and castle long, as against the King's Indian. (The same set-up comes after 1...d6 2.e4 g6.)

lines.title: The Benoni: 1...c5 2.d5
lines.intro: Black hits d4 with the c-pawn on move one. Push past with d5, then Nc3, e4, Nf3, Be2 and castle. You get more space and an easy game. (After 1...Nf6 2.Nc3 c5 push 3.d5 too: the game is often the same.)

lines.title: Philidor set-up: 1...d6 2.e4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5
lines.intro: Black plays ...d6, ...Nf6, ...e5 and ...Nbd7: solid, but a little passive. Take the centre with e4, then Nf3, Bc4 and castle short. Remember: a4 stops ...b5, h3 stops ...Ng4.

lines.title: The Dutch: 1...f5
lines.intro: Black plays 1...f5 to control e4. Answer with Nc3 and Bg5: you take on f6 and Black's pawns become clumsy. About equal, but Black's position is harder to play.

lines.title: The Dutch: 3...e6?! 4.e4!
lines.intro: In the Dutch, Black answers 3.Bg5 with ...e6 instead of ...d5. That leaves e4 unguarded by a pawn: break with e4 at once. After the swaps you win a pawn and Black's king is stuck in the middle.

lines.title: The Stonewall Dutch: 1...f5 2.Nc3 d5
lines.intro: Black puts pawns on d5, e6 and f5: the Stonewall. The hole on e5 is yours. Play Bf4 and e3, jump to b5 and take the d6 bishop, then castle and push c4. (The same position comes from 1...d5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Bf4 f5 4.e3 Nf6: you met that once.)

lines.title: 1...b6: the big centre
lines.intro: Black plays ...b6 and ...Bb7 and leaves the centre to you. Take it with e4 at once, then Nc3, Bd3, Nge2 and castle. (The same set-up comes after 1...e6 2.Nc3 b6 3.e4.) White is clearly better.

lines.title: 1...e6 2.Nc3 c5: push past with d5
lines.intro: Black hits d4 with the c-pawn before playing ...d5. Push your pawn to d5, and after the swaps your queen and pieces get very active. White is clearly better.

lines.title: 1...e6 2.Nc3 Bb4
lines.intro: Black pins your knight on move two. Use the same answer as always: Qd3. If Black swaps on c3 and trades queens, you have the two bishops in a calm endgame.

lines.title: The Englund Gambit: 1...e5?
lines.intro: Black gives up a pawn on move one. Take it, guard it with Nf3, and do not fall for the queen trick on b4: play Nc3 before Bf4. You stay a pawn up with a big lead in development.

courses.title: Caro-Kann Defence
courses.sub: 1.e4 c6 and 2...d5 against everything: a solid repertoire where your light-squared bishop gets out before ...e6
courses.why: The Caro-Kann is already your most-played answer to 1.e4, and it suits you: the pawn on c6 supports ...d5, your pawn structure stays healthy, and the plans repeat from line to line. In your games White most often plays 2.d4 (25 games), then 2.Nf3 (18), 2.Bc4 (5), 2.Qf3 and 2.f4 (2 each); every one of them is in this course. Against best play White keeps a small edge, as in every opening for Black, but your positions have no weak points and endgames are good for you.

ideas.text: Your light-squared bishop goes to f5 (or g4) before the e-pawn moves. If you play ...e6 first, the bishop is locked inside your own pawns for the whole game.
After 3.e5 Bf5 and ...e6, attack White's d4 pawn, the base of the pawn chain (the diagonal row of pawns d4-e5): ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Knights go to e7 and then f5 or g6.
Against h4 answer ...h5 so the pawn cannot go on to h5. Against an early g4 jump to e4 with the bishop. Otherwise step back to g6 and hit back with ...c5 or ...h5.
After exd5 cxd5: knights to c6 and f6, bishop to g4 or f5, then ...e6 and ...Bd6. Against a check on b5 block with ...Bd7. When your bishop has left c8, watch the b7 pawn: White's queen likes b3.

ideas.t: Classical: a home for the bishop
ideas.text: After 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5.Ng3 Bg6: answer h4 with ...h6, so the bishop has the h7 square. Then ...Nd7, ...Ngf6, ...e6, develop the bishop from f8 and castle.
If White does not play d4 early (2.Bc4, 2.Qf3, 2.d3), take the centre with ...d5 and, where it is safe, ...e5 as well.
The Caro-Kann pawn structure has no weak pawns. Do not be afraid of a queen trade: the endgame is usually comfortable or better for you.

structures.text: White has more space on the kingside thanks to the pawn on e5. Your bishop is already outside the chain on f5, so you are not cramped. Attack the base of the chain on d4 with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Knights belong on e7 and f5 or g6, where they press on d4.

Both sides have a pawn in the middle and the c-file is half open for you. White may use the e5 square and the e-file. You develop calmly: knights to c6 and f6, bishop to g4 or f5, ...e6 and ...Bd6. Later you can push ...b5-b4 on the queenside to create a weakness in White's camp.

structures.t: Classical: c6 and e6 against d4
structures.text: You have no pawn in the middle, but your pawns on c6 and e6 cover d5, so White's pieces have no good squares there. Develop, castle and then free your game with the pawn break ...c5 (or ...e5). Trades help you: the endgame is very solid for you.

White's d4 pawn has no pawns next to it (an isolated pawn): it cannot be protected by another pawn. Block it by keeping a piece on d5, the square in front of it. Trade minor pieces: the fewer pieces on the board, the weaker the lonely pawn becomes.

chapters.title: Advance Variation: quiet set-ups (3.e5 Bf5)
chapters.intro: White pushes the pawn to e5 and grabs space. You answer with the Caro-Kann rule: bishop out to f5 first, then ...e6, and then attack d4 with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Your bishop is outside the pawn chain, so you get a good French Defence.

chapters.title: Advance Variation: White chases the bishop
chapters.intro: Here White uses pawns or pieces to attack your bishop on f5. The rules: against h4 play ...h5 so the pawn cannot go on; against an early g4 jump to e4 with the bishop; otherwise step back to g6 and hit back with ...c5 or ...h5.

chapters.title: Classical: 3.Nc3 (or 3.Nd2) dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5
chapters.intro: When White guards e4 with a knight, take the pawn and develop the bishop with a threat. The bishop needs a safe home: answer h4 with ...h6, so it can sit on h7. Then ...Nd7, ...e6, ...Ngf6, the f8 bishop out and castle. The same position comes after 3.Nd2 dxe4 4.Nxe4.

chapters.title: Exchange and Panov: 3.exd5 cxd5
chapters.intro: White swaps on d5 and you take back with the c-pawn. Develop with ...Nc6 and ...Nf6, get the bishop out to g4 or f5, then ...e6. Against a check on b5 block with ...Bd7. When your bishop has left c8, watch your b7 pawn: White's queen likes the b3 square.

chapters.title: 2.Nf3 and 2.Nc3: the Two Knights and friends
chapters.intro: Your most common sideline: 2.Nf3 came in 18 of your games. After 2...d5 White can push, swap, or play Nc3. Your bishop goes to g4 here: it pins the knight and will often take it. The same rules apply: bishop out before ...e6, and against a check on b5 block with ...Bd7.

chapters.title: Sidelines: Fantasy, 2.Bc4, 2.Qf3, 2.f4, 2.c4 and 2.d3
chapters.intro: White avoids the main lines. The rules stay the same: ...d5 against everything, bishop out before ...e6, and if White gives you the centre, take it.

lines.title: Short system: 5.Be2 c5 6.O-O

lines.intro: White guards d4 with the bishop instead of castling. Swap on d4 at once and hit the knight that takes back. Remember: if the queen pins your knight from a4, answer with ...a6 and ...dxc4, then offer the queen trade with ...Qa5.

lines.title: 5.c3 c5 6.Be3: the queen to b6
lines.intro: White supports d4 with c3 and the bishop on e3. Hit b2 with ...Qb6, then close the queenside with ...c4 and expand with ...b5. Remember: when White's bishop leaves c1, b2 is often weak.

lines.title: 4.Nf3 e6 5.Bd3: swap and hit d4
lines.intro: White offers the bishop trade after Nf3. Take it, strike at d4 with ...c5, and develop the knights to d7 and e7-f5. Remember: the knight on f5 is your best piece in this structure.

lines.title: 4.Bd3: swap bishops, then ...Qb6-a6
lines.intro: White offers to trade the light-squared bishops at once. Take it, then attack d4 and bring your queen to a6 to offer a queen trade on the light squares. Remember: Bxd3, ...e6, ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6-a6.

lines.title: 4.Nd2: the knight goes to b3
lines.intro: White wants Nb3 to control c5 and stop your ...c5. Prepare it with ...Nd7, push ...c5 anyway, and win the piece back with a queen check. Remember: ...Qa5+ before taking back on c5.

lines.title: 4.h3?!: White prepares g4
lines.intro: White spends a move to prepare g4 against your bishop. Stay calm: ...e6 and ...c5 as usual. If the g-pawn comes, the bishop steps back to g6. You met this three times and won all three games.

lines.title: 4.Nc3 e6 5.Nf3
lines.intro: White develops normally instead of chasing your bishop. You swap the light-squared bishops, attack d4 with ...c5 and use the open c-file. Remember: ...Nd7 first, then ...c5. (The same position comes from 4.Nf3 e6 5.Nc3.)

lines.title: 4.Nc3 e6 5.Bd3
lines.intro: White offers the bishop trade at once. Develop the knight to e7 first, then swap, so the knight can jump to f5. Remember: ...Ne7, ...Bxd3, ...Nf5 and ...h5 to keep the knight there.

lines.title: 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4: the sharpest line
lines.intro: White throws the g- and h-pawns at your bishop. Retreat to g6, hit the centre with ...c5, meet h4 with ...h5 and give the h-pawn back for fast development. This is the sharpest line of the course: learn every move.

lines.title: 4.h4 h5!: stop the pawn
lines.intro: White pushes the h-pawn to chase your bishop with h5 and g4 later. Answer at once with ...h5: the pawn is stopped and g4 can always be met. Remember: never ...e6 before ...h5 here.

lines.title: 4.g4 Be4!: dodge the pawns
lines.intro: White throws the g-pawn at your bishop at once. Jump to e4: the bishop attacks the rook on h1, so White has to spend another pawn move. Remember: ...Be4, ...Bg6, then ...h5 against h4.

lines.title: 4.c4: White hits d5
lines.intro: White attacks your d5 pawn with the c-pawn. Keep the centre with ...e6 and ...Ne7, take back on d5 with the knight and then trade the light-squared bishops. Remember: do not take on c4: that only helps White develop.

lines.title: Main line: 6.h4 h6 7.Nf3 Nd7 8.h5
lines.intro: White's most testing plan: chase your bishop with the h-pawn and castle long. Remember the order: ...h6 (home for the bishop), ...Nd7 (stops Ne5), then trade bishops and develop.

lines.title: 11.Bf4: check on a5 and trade bishops
lines.intro: In the main line White sometimes puts the bishop on f4 instead of d2. Give a check on a5, block with the bishop on b4 and trade the dark-squared bishops. Remember: ...Qa5+ then ...Bb4.

lines.title: 6.Nf3 Nd7 7.Bd3: no h-pawn attack
lines.intro: Many club players skip the h4 push and simply develop. Play ...Nd7 at once so the knight cannot come to e5, then trade bishops and develop calmly. Remember: if White plays h4 later, ...h6 still gives the bishop its home.

lines.title: 6.Bc4 e6 7.Nf3: watch e6
lines.intro: White aims the bishop at e6 and f7. Close the diagonal with ...e6, develop with ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6, castle, and chase the bishop with ...b5. Remember: e6 is the square White would like to sacrifice on, so keep it guarded.

lines.title: 5.Bd3?!: take the d4 pawn
lines.intro: White guards the knight with the bishop and forgets the d4 pawn. Take it with the queen, bring the queen home and trade pieces. Against the best defence you keep a healthy extra pawn; the position is about level only because White is ahead in development.

lines.title: 5.Bd3?! Qxd4 and 7.O-O?!: the queen trade
lines.intro: After the free pawn on d4, most players at your level castle at once. That leaves the knight on e4 loose: take it, trade queens and enjoy a clean extra pawn in the endgame.

lines.title: Exchange: 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Qc7 6.Ne2
lines.intro: The classical Exchange Variation. Your queen on c7 stops White's bishop from reaching f4, and your bishop goes to g4 before ...e6. Remember: queen on c7 guards b7 against Qb3.

lines.title: Exchange: 6.h3 Nf6 7.Nf3 g6
lines.intro: White plays h3 so that your bishop cannot come to g4. Fianchetto the other bishop instead and bring the knight to f4 via h5. Remember: ...g6, ...Bg7, ...Nh5-f4, castle.

lines.title: Exchange: 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bd3
lines.intro: Your most frequent Black position: 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.d4 (13 of your games); it also comes from 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nf3. Knights to f6 and c6, bishop to g4 with a pin, then ...e6, ...Bd6 and castle. Remember: bishop out before ...e6.

lines.title: Exchange: 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Nc3 Bg4
lines.intro: White develops the queen's knight instead of the bishop. Pin and take the f3 knight, then put all your pieces on d4. Remember: ...Bg4, ...Bxf3, ...Nc6, ...e6, ...Bd6 and ...Qb6. (4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Nf3 is the same position.)

lines.title: Exchange: 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Bf4
lines.intro: White develops the queen's knight first and then the bishop to f4. Stop the knight jump to b5 with ...a6, develop with ...Nc6 and ...Bf5, trade bishops and castle. (After 5.Nf3 you are in line ex-nf3-nc3.)

lines.title: Panov: 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e6 6.Nf3 Bb4
lines.intro: White plays c4 and gets a lonely pawn on d4 after the swaps. Your recipe: pin the c3 knight with ...Bb4, take back on d5 with the knight, castle and keep a piece on d5, the square in front of the d4 pawn.

lines.title: Panov: 7.Bd3 dxc4
lines.intro: White develops the bishop to d3 instead of swapping on d5. Take on c4 so that White's bishop has to move again, castle and put your other bishop on b7, aiming at White's king. Remember: ...dxc4, ...O-O, ...b6 and ...Bb7.

lines.title: Two Knights: 3...Bg4 4.h3 Bxf3
lines.intro: The Two Knights: White develops both knights first. Pin with ...Bg4, take on f3 when asked, and build the c6-d5-e6 wall. Remember: never ...Bh5 here (see the trap).

lines.title: Two Knights: 4.Be2 e6 5.d4
lines.intro: White does not ask the bishop with h3 at once. Close the centre with ...e6, develop the queen's knight to d7, and swap on e4 when White castles. Remember: after White's knight leaves f3, your bishop on h5 is attacked by the bishop on e2.

lines.title: Two Knights: 4.exd5 cxd5 5.d4
lines.intro: White swaps on d5 first and then plays d4. You get a solid Exchange-type centre with your bishop already outside. Remember: take on f3 when White asks with h3, then attack d4 and trade the dark-squared bishops with ...g6 and ...Bh6.

lines.title: 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5 Bg4 4.d4 e6 5.Be2
lines.intro: White pushes e5 before d4. Your bishop goes to g4 (not f5) and pins the knight. It is an Advance Variation where the bishop is already outside. Remember: ...c5, swap on d4, and trade bishops as soon as White's knight leaves f3.

lines.title: 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5 Bg4 4.d4 e6 5.h3
lines.intro: White asks your bishop at once. Take the knight, hit d4 with ...c5 and ...Qb6, and grab the pawns White leaves behind. Remember: after the swap on f3, White's queen no longer guards d4.

lines.title: 5.Be2 c5 6.h3?: d4 falls
lines.intro: After ...c5, many White players ask your bishop with h3. That is a mistake: you take on f3, swap on d4, and White's e5 pawn has lost its support.

lines.title: 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bb5+ Bd7
lines.intro: White swaps on d5 and gives a check on b5 before d4. Block with the bishop (the standard answer to a check on b5), take back on d7 with the knight and develop. Remember: ...Bd7, ...Nxd7, ...Ngf6, ...Rc8 and ...e6.

lines.title: 2.Nf3 d5 3.d3: trade queens
lines.intro: White plays a slow d3. Swap pawns on e4 and trade queens: White's king loses the right to castle and you get a comfortable endgame. Remember: endgames are good for the Caro-Kann.

lines.title: 2.Nf3 d5 3.c3?: take the pawn
lines.intro: White plays c3 as if d4 were coming, but the e4 pawn hangs. Take it. The knight cannot win it back, and you end up a clean pawn ahead.

lines.title: Fantasy Variation: 3.f3 e6 4.Nc3 Bb4
lines.intro: White guards e4 with the f-pawn. Keep it solid: ...e6 and pin the knight with ...Bb4. Later trade on c3, take on e4 and develop your last bishop with ...b6. Remember: here your light-squared bishop comes out late, via b7 or a6.

lines.title: 2.f4?!: the Advance with f4
lines.intro: White pushes the f-pawn first and then plays e5. You get an Advance Variation where White's f-pawn blocks the bishop on c1. Remember: ...Bf5, ...e6, ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and ...h5 against g4. (The same position comes from 3.e5 Bf5 4.f4.)

lines.title: 2.Bc4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bb5+
lines.intro: After the swap on d5 White's bishop gives a check on b5. Block with your bishop (the standard answer to a check on b5), take back with the queen and set up ...e6, ...Nc6, ...Nge7-f5. Remember: you are already slightly better here, because White's bishop has moved three times.

lines.title: 2.Qf3?!: the early queen
lines.intro: White brings the queen out on move two. Take the centre with ...d5, develop with tempo against the queen, and you get the bishop pair. Remember: ...Bg4 hits the queen.

lines.title: 2.Qf3 d5 3.d4: take on e4
lines.intro: After the early queen White can also defend nothing and play d4. Take on e4, develop with tempo against the queen and fianchetto the bishop on g7. Remember: the queen is a target, so every developing move that hits it gains time.

lines.title: 2.c4 d5: White swaps twice on d5
lines.intro: White plays c4 at once and takes on d5 twice. Do not hurry to take back with the queen: develop the knight, win the pawn back and fianchetto the bishop. If White plays d4 instead, you are in the Panov. (The same position can come from 1.c4 c6 2.e4.)

traps.intro: After 4.h3 almost half the players at your level keep the pin with ...Bh5. That walks into a famous trap: a check on b5 pins your knight and g4 and Ne5 win material. Take on f3 instead.

traps.title: Classical: 5.f3 and the bishop swap
traps.intro: White kicks your knight-hunting bishop with the f-pawn idea instead of moving the knight. Many players swap on e4, which only helps White build a big centre. Develop with ...Nf6 and let White decide.

traps.title: 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3: the f7 trap
traps.intro: White leaves the e4 pawn and aims everything at f7. Take the pawn, and after the queen comes to h5 guard f7 with ...e6. Never answer with the natural knight move to f6 here.

notes.10: The queen goes to c7, as in line ex-main: it covers f4 and guards b7 in advance.
notes.14: When White's bishop comes to f4, Black strikes in the centre with ...e5, the same idea as in line ex-main.

notes.16: After h3 has stopped ...Bg4, Black fianchettoes with ...g6, the plan of line ex-h3.
notes.18: The light-squared bishop comes out to f5 and offers a trade of bishops.
